Direct integrals of von Neumann algebras

Written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), September 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI. Original text: CC0 1.0.

A direct integral of Hilbert spaces H=∫Γ⊕H(γ) dμ(γ)\mathcal H=\int_\Gamma^\oplus H(\gamma)\,d\mu(\gamma)H=∫Γ⊕​H(γ)dμ(γ) comes with two von Neumann algebras of its own. The diagonal algebra A\mathcal AA multiplies every fibre by a scalar that varies measurably with the point. The decomposable algebra D\mathcal DD acts on every fibre by a bounded operator. Each of the two is the commutant of the other. Many algebras lie between them. Pick, at each point γ\gammaγ, a von Neumann algebra M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) on the fibre H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ), and keep the decomposable operators whose fibres lie in M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) at almost every point. The resulting set is written ∫Γ⊕M(γ) dμ(γ)\int_\Gamma^\oplus M(\gamma)\,d\mu(\gamma)∫Γ⊕​M(γ)dμ(γ).

This lesson studies that construction. When the family γ↦M(γ)\gamma\mapsto M(\gamma)γ↦M(γ) is measurable, in the sense of Section 1, the set is a von Neumann algebra. Its commutant is obtained by integrating the commutants M(γ)′M(\gamma)'M(γ)′, and its centre by integrating the centres M(γ)∩M(γ)′M(\gamma)\cap M(\gamma)'M(γ)∩M(γ)′ (Theorems 3.2 and 4.3). So the centre equals the diagonal algebra exactly when almost all the M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) are factors. The family can be recovered from its integral, up to a null set (Theorem 4.1). Conversely, every von Neumann algebra that contains A\mathcal AA and is contained in D\mathcal DD arises in this way (Theorem 5.3). Measurable families, taken up to null sets, therefore match the von Neumann algebras between A\mathcal AA and D\mathcal DD one to one.

These facts form the core of von Neumann's reduction theory (1949); see [Blackadar, Section III.1.6]. After a von Neumann algebra has been written as an integral over an abelian subalgebra of its centre, many questions about it become questions about the fibres. When the whole centre is used, the fibres are factors. The delicate point is measurability. That the fields of commutants and of centres are again measurable rests on the Borel space of von Neumann algebras introduced in [Effros 1965].

The base is an arbitrary σ\sigmaσ-finite measure space throughout. We need no standard Borel structure, no completeness of the measure and no separability of H\mathcal HH. Section 6 explains where standard bases will matter later. It also gives a base on which a harmless-looking family is not measurable, and on which the commutant formula fails for it.

We assume the lessons Measurable fields of Hilbert spaces and their direct integrals, Decomposable operators and the diagonal algebra and The Effros Borel structure. Every fact we take from them is stated in full in the section Background used without proof. Example 7.2 also uses Spatial tensor products of von Neumann algebras.

Basic references are [Takesaki I, Chapter IV] and [Blackadar, Section III.1.6].

Conventions

Throughout, (Γ,Σ,μ)(\Gamma,\Sigma,\mu)(Γ,Σ,μ) is a σ\sigmaσ-finite measure space, and measurable means Σ\SigmaΣ-measurable. We assume nothing about completeness of μ\muμ, standardness of (Γ,Σ)(\Gamma,\Sigma)(Γ,Σ) or countability properties of Σ\SigmaΣ. A null set is a set N∈ΣN\in\SigmaN∈Σ with μ(N)=0\mu(N)=0μ(N)=0. A statement holds almost everywhere, or for almost every γ\gammaγ, if it holds for all γ\gammaγ outside some null set. A subset E⊆ΓE\subseteq\GammaE⊆Γ is measurable up to a null set if some F∈ΣF\in\SigmaF∈Σ has E △ FE\,\triangle\,FE△F contained in a null set. When Σ\SigmaΣ is complete for μ\muμ, these are the familiar notions.

Hilbert spaces are complex, inner products are linear in the first variable, and the zero space is allowed. For a Hilbert space KKK, B(K)B(K)B(K) is the algebra of bounded operators on KKK, and S′S'S′ is the commutant of a set S⊆B(K)S\subseteq B(K)S⊆B(K). A von Neumann algebra on KKK is a ∗*∗-subalgebra M⊆B(K)M\subseteq B(K)M⊆B(K) with M′′=MM''=MM′′=M. The von Neumann algebra generated by a set SSS is (S∪S∗)′′(S\cup S^*)''(S∪S∗)′′. The centre of MMM is M∩M′M\cap M'M∩M′, and MMM is a factor if its centre is C1\mathbb C1C1. For von Neumann algebras M1,M2M_1,M_2M1​,M2​ on KKK we put M1∨M2=(M1∪M2)′′M_1\vee M_2=(M_1\cup M_2)''M1​∨M2​=(M1​∪M2​)′′. On the zero space, B(0)={0}=C1B(0)=\{0\}=\mathbb C1B(0)={0}=C1 is the only von Neumann algebra, and it is a factor by this definition.

We use four elementary facts about commutants. Let S,T⊆B(K)S,T\subseteq B(K)S,T⊆B(K).

  • (C1) If S⊆TS\subseteq TS⊆T, then T′⊆S′T'\subseteq S'T′⊆S′. Also S⊆S′′S\subseteq S''S⊆S′′, and hence S′′′=S′S'''=S'S′′′=S′.

  • (C3) The von Neumann algebra generated by SSS is the smallest von Neumann algebra containing SSS, and its commutant is (S∪S∗)′(S\cup S^*)'(S∪S∗)′.
  • (C4) If M1,M2M_1,M_2M1​,M2​ are von Neumann algebras, then M1∩M2=(M1′∪M2′)′M_1\cap M_2=(M_1'\cup M_2')'M1​∩M2​=(M1′​∪M2′​)′ is a von Neumann algebra. Proof. (C1) An operator that commutes with all of TTT commutes with all of SSS. Every element of SSS commutes with every element of S′S'S′, so S⊆S′′S\subseteq S''S⊆S′′. Applying the first statement to S⊆S′′S\subseteq S''S⊆S′′ gives S′′′⊆S′S'''\subseteq S'S′′′⊆S′, and applying the second to S′S'S′ gives S′⊆S′′′S'\subseteq S'''S′⊆S′′′.

(C2) Sums and products of operators that commute with SSS commute with SSS, and so does 111. Let S∗=SS^*=SS∗=S and x∈S′x\in S'x∈S′. For s∈Ss\in Ss∈S we have xs∗=s∗xxs^*=s^*xxs∗=s∗x, and taking adjoints gives sx∗=x∗ssx^*=x^*ssx∗=x∗s. So x∗∈S′x^*\in S'x∗∈S′, and S′S'S′ is a ∗*∗-algebra. It equals its own bicommutant by (C1).

1. Measurable fields of von Neumann algebras

Definition 1.1. A field of von Neumann algebras on (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)) is a family M=(M(γ))γ∈ΓM=(M(\gamma))_{\gamma\in\Gamma}M=(M(γ))γ∈Γ​ in which each M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is a von Neumann algebra acting on H(γ)H(\gamma)H(γ). The field is measurable if there are measurable operator fields x1,x2,…x_1,x_2,\ldotsx1​,x2​,… on (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)) such that, for almost every γ\gammaγ, the algebra M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is generated by {xj(γ):j≥1}\{x_j(\gamma):j\geq1\}{xj​(γ):j≥1}. Two fields are equivalent if they agree almost everywhere.

The generating fields need not be essentially bounded; their norms may grow without bound. Finitely many generators are allowed: repeat one of them. For a field MMM we write M′M'M′ for the field (M(γ)′)(M(\gamma)')(M(γ)′) of commutants and ZMZ_MZM​ for the field (M(γ)∩M(γ)′)(M(\gamma)\cap M(\gamma)')(M(γ)∩M(γ)′) of centres. For two fields M1,M2M_1,M_2M1​,M2​ we write M1∩M2M_1\cap M_2M1​∩M2​ and M1∨M2M_1\vee M_2M1​∨M2​ for the fields (M1(γ)∩M2(γ))(M_1(\gamma)\cap M_2(\gamma))(M1​(γ)∩M2​(γ)) and (M1(γ)∨M2(γ))(M_1(\gamma)\vee M_2(\gamma))(M1​(γ)∨M2​(γ)). By (C2) and (C4), these are again fields of von Neumann algebras.

A measurably generated family in the sense of (B11) is a measurable field. The only difference is the null set: Proposition 1.3(1) shows that every measurable field is equivalent to a measurably generated family.

Remark 1.4.

  1. Every von Neumann algebra PPP acting on a separable space KKK is generated by a countable set. Indeed, by (B10) the unit ball of PPP lies in a compact metrizable space, so it has a countable σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense subset SSS. The von Neumann algebra generated by SSS is a commutant, hence σ\sigmaσ-weakly closed (B10). It contains SSS, hence the unit ball of PPP, hence PPP; and it lies in PPP by (C3). So measurability is not about the number of generators at one point. It asks that the generators be chosen measurably in γ\gammaγ.
  2. A field that is equivalent to a measurable field is measurable, since the same generating fields serve outside a null set.
  3. By (B10), the maps Φd\Phi_dΦd​ of Proposition 1.3(5) take values in standard Borel spaces. So a measurable field is, up to a null set, a measurable map from each dimension stratum into a standard Borel space of von Neumann algebras.

3. The commutant theorem

Lemma 3.1.

  1. Let xxx be an essentially bounded measurable operator field, and let T=∫⊕t∈DT=\int^\oplus t\in\mathcal DT=∫⊕t∈D. Then TTT commutes with ∫⊕x\int^\oplus x∫⊕x if and only if t(γ)x(γ)=x(γ)t(γ)t(\gamma)x(\gamma)=x(\gamma)t(\gamma)t(γ)x(γ)=x(γ)t(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ.
  2. (Truncation) Let xxx be a measurable operator field and m≥1m\geq1m≥1. Then x[m]=1{∥x∥≤m} xx^{[m]}=1_{\{\|x\|\leq m\}}\,xx[m]=1{∥x∥≤m}​x is a measurable operator field with ∥x[m](γ)∥≤m\|x^{[m]}(\gamma)\|\leq m∥x[m](γ)∥≤m for every γ\gammaγ, and x[m](γ)=x(γ)x^{[m]}(\gamma)=x(\gamma)x[m](γ)=x(γ) whenever ∥x(γ)∥≤m\|x(\gamma)\|\leq m∥x(γ)∥≤m. If MMM is a field of von Neumann algebras with x(γ)∈M(γ)x(\gamma)\in M(\gamma)x(γ)∈M(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ, then ∫⊕x[m]\int^\oplus x^{[m]}∫⊕x[m] and its adjoint lie in ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M.

Proof. (1) By (B4), T∫⊕x−(∫⊕x)T=∫⊕(tx−xt)T\int^\oplus x-(\int^\oplus x)T=\int^\oplus(tx-xt)T∫⊕x−(∫⊕x)T=∫⊕(tx−xt). The field tx−xttx-xttx−xt is measurable and essentially bounded by (B3). By (B4), it defines the zero operator exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere.

(2) The norm function of xxx is measurable (B3), so 1{∥x∥≤m}1_{\{\|x\|\leq m\}}1{∥x∥≤m}​ is a measurable function and x[m]x^{[m]}x[m] is a measurable operator field (B3). The bound and the equality are clear. Where x(γ)∈M(γ)x(\gamma)\in M(\gamma)x(γ)∈M(γ), the operator x[m](γ)x^{[m]}(\gamma)x[m](γ), which is x(γ)x(\gamma)x(γ) or 000, lies in M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ). So ∫⊕x[m]∈∫⊕M\int^\oplus x^{[m]}\in\int^\oplus M∫⊕x[m]∈∫⊕M, and its adjoint lies there too by Proposition 2.2(2). □\square□

Theorem 3.2 (Commutant theorem). Let MMM be a measurable field on (H(γ))(H(\gamma))(H(γ)), as in Definition 1.1.

  1. (∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M′\big(\int^\oplus M\big)'=\int^\oplus M'(∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M′.
  2. ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M is a von Neumann algebra acting on H\mathcal HH, and its centre contains the diagonal algebra A\mathcal AA.
  3. ∫⊕M′\int^\oplus M'∫⊕M′ is also a von Neumann algebra, with commutant (∫⊕M′)′=∫⊕M\big(\int^\oplus M'\big)'=\int^\oplus M(∫⊕M′)′=∫⊕M.

Proof. (1) The inclusion ⊇\supseteq⊇. Let S∈∫⊕M′S\in\int^\oplus M'S∈∫⊕M′ and T∈∫⊕MT\in\int^\oplus MT∈∫⊕M. Write S=∫⊕sS=\int^\oplus sS=∫⊕s and T=∫⊕tT=\int^\oplus tT=∫⊕t, with s(γ)∈M(γ)′s(\gamma)\in M(\gamma)'s(γ)∈M(γ)′ and t(γ)∈M(γ)t(\gamma)\in M(\gamma)t(γ)∈M(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ. Then s(γ)t(γ)=t(γ)s(γ)s(\gamma)t(\gamma)=t(\gamma)s(\gamma)s(γ)t(γ)=t(γ)s(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ, and Lemma 3.1(1) gives ST=TSST=TSST=TS. This part holds for every field MMM.

Theorem 5.3 (Von Neumann algebras between A\mathcal AA and D\mathcal DD). Let B\mathcal BB be a von Neumann algebra on H\mathcal HH. Then B=∫⊕M\mathcal B=\int^\oplus MB=∫⊕M for some measurable field MMM if and only if A⊆B⊆D\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal DA⊆B⊆D. In that case:

Proof. If B=∫⊕M\mathcal B=\int^\oplus MB=∫⊕M with MMM measurable, then A⊆B⊆D\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal DA⊆B⊆D by Proposition 2.2(2). Conversely, let A⊆B⊆D\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal DA⊆B⊆D. Lemma 5.2 gives a countable S0⊆BS_0\subseteq\mathcal BS0​⊆B such that B\mathcal BB is generated by A∪S0\mathcal A\cup S_0A∪S0​, and Lemma 5.1 gives B=∫⊕MS0\mathcal B=\int^\oplus M_{S_0}B=∫⊕MS0​​. This proves the equivalence and (3). Part (1) is Theorem 4.1, and part (2) is Theorems 3.2(1) and 4.3. □\square□

Remark 5.4 (The separable case). If H\mathcal HH is separable, Lemma 5.2 is immediate. By (B10), the unit ball of B(H)B(\mathcal H)B(H) is compact and metrizable in the σ\sigmaσ-weak topology. So the unit ball of B\mathcal BB has a countable σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense subset S0S_0S0​, and S0S_0S0​ generates B\mathcal BB by the argument of Remark 1.4(1). The essential supremum in the proof of Lemma 5.2 replaces the separability of H\mathcal HH by that of the fibres. This matters when H\mathcal HH is not separable, which can happen when Σ\SigmaΣ is not countably generated up to null sets (Remark 3.3(2)).

Proof. The map is well defined and preserves inclusion by Proposition 2.2(3); it is injective and reflects inclusion by Theorem 4.1; and it is onto by Theorem 5.3. The four items are Theorem 3.2(1), Proposition 2.2(4), Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 2.2(5). □\square□

Joins are treated in Exercise 8.3.

6. Standard and non-standard bases

Remark 6.1. Sections 1 to 5 hold over every σ\sigmaσ-finite measure space. In particular they hold when Σ\SigmaΣ is the Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra of a standard Borel space, and also when Σ\SigmaΣ is its completion for μ\muμ, which is the setting of μ\muμ-measurable fields. Standard bases matter for two later questions. How can a given abelian von Neumann algebra be realized as a diagonal algebra? And is the base of such a realization determined by the algebra? Corollary 6.2 collects what the standard case adds, and Example 6.3 shows what can go wrong without it.

Corollary 6.2 (Standard bases). Let Γ\GammaΓ be a standard Borel space, Σ\SigmaΣ its Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra, and μ\muμ a σ\sigmaσ-finite measure on Σ\SigmaΣ.

  1. H\mathcal HH is separable.
  2. A field MMM of von Neumann algebras is measurable exactly when, for each ddd, the map γ↦U(γ)M(γ)U(γ)∗\gamma\mapsto U(\gamma)M(\gamma)U(\gamma)^*γ↦U(γ)M(γ)U(γ)∗ agrees almost everywhere on Γd\Gamma_dΓd​ with a Borel map into the standard Borel space vN(ℓd2)\mathrm{vN}(\ell^2_d)vN(ℓd2​).
  3. Let B\mathcal BB be a von Neumann algebra with A⊆B⊆D\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal DA⊆B⊆D. There is a sequence (bk)(b_k)(bk​) that is σ\sigmaσ-weakly dense in the unit ball of B\mathcal BB. For each kkk choose a representing field βk\beta_kβk​ of bkb_kbk​, and let M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) be the von Neumann algebra generated by {βk(γ):k≥1}\{\beta_k(\gamma):k\geq1\}{βk​(γ):k≥1}. Then B=∫⊕M\mathcal B=\int^\oplus MB=∫⊕M.
  4. For a measurable field MMM, the set of γ\gammaγ where M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is a factor is a Borel set up to a null set, and the centre of ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M is A\mathcal AA exactly when its complement is contained in a null set.

Proof. (1) is (B4). (2) is Proposition 1.3(5) together with (B10). (3) By (1) and Remark 5.4, such a sequence exists and generates B\mathcal BB. Since A⊆B\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal BA⊆B, the set A∪{bk}\mathcal A\cup\{b_k\}A∪{bk​} generates B\mathcal BB as well, and Lemma 5.1 applies. (4) is Proposition 1.3(4) with Theorem 4.3. □\square□

Example 6.3 (A separating σ\sigmaσ-algebra that is not countably generated). Let Γ=[0,1]\Gamma=[0,1]Γ=[0,1]. The Borel sets. Give [0,1][0,1][0,1] its Borel σ\sigmaσ-algebra and Lebesgue measure. The countable–co-countable sets. Now let Σc\Sigma_cΣc​ consist of the countable subsets of [0,1][0,1][0,1] and their complements. Let μc(E)\mu_c(E)μc​(E) be 000 for countable EEE and 111 otherwise. This is a probability measure. The σ\sigmaσ-algebra Σc\Sigma_cΣc​ contains every singleton, so it separates points, and its null sets are the countable sets.

A function f:[0,1]→Cf:[0,1]\to\mathbb Cf:[0,1]→C is Σc\Sigma_cΣc​-measurable exactly when it is constant outside a countable set. Such a function is clearly measurable. Conversely, let fff be measurable and k≥1k\geq1k≥1. Cover C\mathbb CC by countably many disjoint squares of side 2−k2^{-k}2−k. Their preimages are disjoint sets in Σc\Sigma_cΣc​ that cover [0,1][0,1][0,1]. They cannot all be countable, and two of them cannot both be co-countable, so exactly one of them, for a square QkQ_kQk​, is co-countable. Outside one countable set, fff takes its values in every QkQ_kQk​ at once. Two values in QkQ_kQk​ differ by at most 2−k22^{-k}\sqrt22−k2​, so fff is constant outside that countable set.

Consequently, over Σc\Sigma_cΣc​ the measurable sections of the constant field C2\mathbb C^2C2 are the maps that are constant outside a countable set (B5). Now compute. Let T=∫⊕xT=\int^\oplus xT=∫⊕x with x(γ)∈E(γ)x(\gamma)\in\mathcal E(\gamma)x(γ)∈E(γ) outside a countable set. Then xxx equals a constant aaa outside a countable set, so a∈E(γ)a\in\mathcal E(\gamma)a∈E(γ) for all γ\gammaγ outside a countable set, and in particular for two different γ\gammaγ. So aaa is a scalar, and ∫⊕E=A=C1\int^\oplus\mathcal E=\mathcal A=\mathbb C1∫⊕E=A=C1. Since E′=E\mathcal E'=\mathcal EE′=E, also ∫⊕E′=C1\int^\oplus\mathcal E'=\mathbb C1∫⊕E′=C1. But (∫⊕E)′=(C1)′=M2(C)≠C1=∫⊕E′. \Big(\int^\oplus\mathcal E\Big)'=(\mathbb C1)'=M_2(\mathbb C)\neq\mathbb C1=\int^\oplus\mathcal E' . (∫⊕E)′=(C1)′=M2​(C)=C1=∫⊕E′. What the base does not see. Over Σc\Sigma_cΣc​, the diagonal algebra is C1\mathbb C1C1, and the direct integral of the constant field is C2\mathbb C^2C2, exactly as over a single point of mass one. But no bijection exists between a co-countable subset of [0,1][0,1][0,1] and a point. So without standardness, the base of a direct integral cannot be recovered from its diagonal algebra, even up to null sets. For standard σ\sigmaσ-finite bases, an isomorphism between the L∞L^\inftyL∞-algebras does come from a Borel isomorphism of the bases, defined outside null sets [Takesaki I, Lemma IV.8.22]. This is why the uniqueness of disintegrations is stated for standard bases.

8. Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Abelian and maximal abelian direct integrals). Let MMM be a measurable field. Show that ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M is abelian if and only if M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is abelian for almost every γ\gammaγ. Show also that (∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M(\int^\oplus M)'=\int^\oplus M(∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M if and only if M(γ)′=M(γ)M(\gamma)'=M(\gamma)M(γ)′=M(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ.

Solution. A von Neumann algebra PPP is abelian exactly when P⊆P′P\subseteq P'P⊆P′. By Theorem 3.2(1), ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M is abelian if and only if ∫⊕M⊆∫⊕M′\int^\oplus M\subseteq\int^\oplus M'∫⊕M⊆∫⊕M′. By Theorem 4.1, applied to the measurable field MMM and to L=M′L=M'L=M′, this holds if and only if M(γ)⊆M(γ)′M(\gamma)\subseteq M(\gamma)'M(γ)⊆M(γ)′ for almost every γ\gammaγ, that is, if and only if M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is abelian for almost every γ\gammaγ. For the second claim, (∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M′(\int^\oplus M)'=\int^\oplus M'(∫⊕M)′=∫⊕M′ by Theorem 3.2(1), and the fields MMM and M′M'M′ are both measurable (Proposition 1.3(3)). By Theorem 4.1, ∫⊕M′=∫⊕M\int^\oplus M'=\int^\oplus M∫⊕M′=∫⊕M if and only if M(γ)′=M(γ)M(\gamma)'=M(\gamma)M(γ)′=M(γ) for almost every γ\gammaγ. Examples 7.3 and 7.4, and Example 6.3 over the Borel sets, are instances of the second claim.

Exercise 8.3 (Joins). Let M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​ be measurable fields. Show that ∫⊕(M1∨M2)=∫⊕M1∨∫⊕M2\int^\oplus(M_1\vee M_2)=\int^\oplus M_1\vee\int^\oplus M_2∫⊕(M1​∨M2​)=∫⊕M1​∨∫⊕M2​, where the right side is the von Neumann algebra generated by the two direct integrals.

Solution. The field M1∨M2M_1\vee M_2M1​∨M2​ is measurable (Proposition 1.3(3)), so its direct integral is a von Neumann algebra (Theorem 3.2(2)); so are ∫⊕M1\int^\oplus M_1∫⊕M1​ and ∫⊕M2\int^\oplus M_2∫⊕M2​. By (C4), Theorem 3.2(1) and Proposition 2.2(4), (∫⊕M1∨∫⊕M2)′=(∫⊕M1)′∩(∫⊕M2)′=∫⊕M1′∩∫⊕M2′=∫⊕(M1′∩M2′). \Big(\int^\oplus M_1\vee\int^\oplus M_2\Big)'=\Big(\int^\oplus M_1\Big)'\cap\Big(\int^\oplus M_2\Big)'=\int^\oplus M_1'\cap\int^\oplus M_2'=\int^\oplus(M_1'\cap M_2'). (∫⊕M1​∨∫⊕M2​)′=(∫⊕M1​)′∩(∫⊕M2​)′=∫⊕M1′​∩∫⊕M2′​=∫⊕(M1′​∩M2′​). By (C4) at each point, M1(γ)′∩M2(γ)′=(M1(γ)∨M2(γ))′M_1(\gamma)'\cap M_2(\gamma)'=(M_1(\gamma)\vee M_2(\gamma))'M1​(γ)′∩M2​(γ)′=(M1​(γ)∨M2​(γ))′. So the last term is ∫⊕(M1∨M2)′\int^\oplus(M_1\vee M_2)'∫⊕(M1​∨M2​)′, which equals (∫⊕(M1∨M2))′(\int^\oplus(M_1\vee M_2))'(∫⊕(M1​∨M2​))′ by Theorem 3.2(1). Two von Neumann algebras with the same commutant are equal, since each is the commutant of its commutant.

Exercise 8.4 (Central projections). Let MMM be a measurable field. Show that a projection PPP on H\mathcal HH lies in the centre of ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M if and only if P=∫⊕pP=\int^\oplus pP=∫⊕p for a measurable operator field ppp such that p(γ)p(\gamma)p(γ) is a projection in the centre of M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) for every γ\gammaγ. Deduce that if almost every M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) is a factor, the central projections of ∫⊕M\int^\oplus M∫⊕M are exactly the operators m1Em_{1_E}m1E​​, E∈ΣE\in\SigmaE∈Σ.

Solution. If ppp is such a field, then ∥p(γ)∥≤1\|p(\gamma)\|\leq1∥p(γ)∥≤1, and P=∫⊕pP=\int^\oplus pP=∫⊕p lies in ∫⊕ZM\int^\oplus Z_M∫⊕ZM​, which is the centre (Theorem 4.3). By (B4), P∗=∫⊕p∗=PP^*=\int^\oplus p^*=PP∗=∫⊕p∗=P and P2=∫⊕p2=PP^2=\int^\oplus p^2=PP2=∫⊕p2=P, so PPP is a projection. Conversely, let PPP be a central projection. By Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 2.2(1), P=∫⊕xP=\int^\oplus xP=∫⊕x with x(γ)x(\gamma)x(γ) in the centre of M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) for every γ\gammaγ. From P=P∗PP=P^*PP=P∗P and (B4), x(γ)=x(γ)∗x(γ)x(\gamma)=x(\gamma)^*x(\gamma)x(γ)=x(γ)∗x(γ) outside a null set NNN. Put p=1Γ∖N xp=1_{\Gamma\setminus N}\,xp=1Γ∖N​x. Then p(γ)=p(γ)∗p(γ)p(\gamma)=p(\gamma)^*p(\gamma)p(γ)=p(γ)∗p(γ) for every γ\gammaγ. Taking adjoints gives p(γ)∗=p(γ)p(\gamma)^*=p(\gamma)p(γ)∗=p(γ), and then p(γ)2=p(γ)p(\gamma)^2=p(\gamma)p(γ)2=p(γ). So each p(γ)p(\gamma)p(γ) is a projection in the centre of M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ), and ∫⊕p=P\int^\oplus p=P∫⊕p=P.

Now let M(γ)M(\gamma)M(γ) be a factor outside a null set N′N'N′. The function c=⟨pe1,e1⟩c=\langle pe_1,e_1\ranglec=⟨pe1​,e1​⟩ is measurable (B1); let E={c=1}E=\{c=1\}E={c=1}. For γ∉N′\gamma\notin N'γ∈/N′ with n(γ)≥1n(\gamma)\geq1n(γ)≥1, p(γ)p(\gamma)p(γ) is a projection in C1\mathbb C1C1, so it is 000 or 111, and it equals c(γ)1=1E(γ)1c(\gamma)1=1_E(\gamma)1c(γ)1=1E​(γ)1. For n(γ)=0n(\gamma)=0n(γ)=0, both sides are the zero operator. So p(γ)=1E(γ)1p(\gamma)=1_E(\gamma)1p(γ)=1E​(γ)1 almost everywhere, and P=m1EP=m_{1_E}P=m1E​​ by (B4) and (B6). Conversely, every m1Em_{1_E}m1E​​ is a projection in A\mathcal AA, which lies in the centre.

Where this leads

  • Disintegration. Let B\mathcal BB be a von Neumann algebra acting on a separable space, and let C\mathcal CC be an abelian von Neumann algebra contained in its centre. Suppose C\mathcal CC has been realized as the diagonal algebra of a direct integral. Then C⊆B⊆C′=D\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal C'=\mathcal DC⊆B⊆C′=D, so Theorem 5.3 writes B\mathcal BB as the direct integral of a measurable field. If C\mathcal CC is the whole centre, almost every fibre is a factor, by Theorem 4.3. How to realize C\mathcal CC as a diagonal algebra over a standard base, and in what sense such a realization is unique, is the subject of a later lesson on disintegration; for a summary, see [Blackadar, III.1.6.3–III.1.6.4].
  • Types. Once an algebra is written as an integral over its centre, the type decomposition of Projections and types of von Neumann algebras can be read fibre by fibre [Blackadar, III.1.6.4].
  • States. For a state of a C*-algebra, the counterpart of the decomposition over the centre is the central measure of Integral representations of states, whose abelian algebra is the centre of the represented algebra.
